utterances.text: I don't know whether they reduced the power, but it's certainly one of the methods to disable the other side from monitoring certain communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that makeshift antennas had a much weaker receiving signal than professional military antennas?

utterances.speaker: RM316: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not agree with you on this point. Professional manufactured military antennas were usable for a much wider range, but if we created an antenna for one specific frequency, then it would be better than a military antenna. Also, military antennas made for one specific frequency were much better than those made for a wide frequency range.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was wind a hindrance in receiving signals?

utterances.speaker: RM316: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wind is not a bother if the antenna is well fixed and the wind does not move it, but if you did not fix the antenna properly, then it will move in the wind, and that will certainly affect reception. That's why we fixed our antenna into one cubic metre of concrete and stabilised it with four steel cables.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know what squelch is?

utterances.speaker: RM316: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That is automatic shutdown of a device due to a disallowed signal.

utterances.speaker: RM316: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we very poor audibility, then we bring the device down to the level of squelch to improve reception, but at the same time, we increase noise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if we give you another two minutes, will you finish?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You will finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm close to the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Let me just ask you this: Do you know what percentage of the signal was not in squelch? In other words, it was admissible for reception, suitable for reception?

utterances.speaker: RM316: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we mounted this parabolic antenna, we had a sufficiently powerful signal, so we did not have to go to the level of noise. It was a perfectly intelligible and good signal, and it was five to ten units, 5S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did you say you mounted that antenna?

utterances.speaker: RM316: Ferid MUSLIĆ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but it's certainly before the events in Srebrenica. At the stage of testing, as soon as we happened upon this frequency, and I think I have it all noted down, that frequency was discovered much earlier. As soon as we detected it, we set about mounting the antenna and identifying a good signal.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir, for answering my questions. That is all I have for you today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. May the Chamber please move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Witness, the Chamber was informed that the Prosecution sees no need to re-examine you, which means that we'll only deal with a very practical matter about associated exhibits. I have a list of five. Are there any objections? And let's perhaps take them one by one. 65 ter 25528. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is the only one we do not object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is provisionally number P1668 was provisionally assigned to it. 65 ter 25528 is admitted as Exhibit P1668. Second one is under seal. The second one, Mr. Lukic, is number 21970. Objections are --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We cannot see who compiled in report, at least it's not visible from the document we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see that. You say it has limited probative value or you say it should therefore not be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would raise both. It shouldn't be admitted, and if it is admitted, it has very limited probative value.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that, of course, is to be assessed in the context of the entirety of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. 65 ter number 21970 is admitted under the number which was provisionally assigned, that is P1669, under seal. I move to the next document, 65 ter 05302. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is only five pages of some handwritten document. We are not clear whether witness knows about all the intercepts entered here or are those his intercepts. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is discussed at transcript page 2080 of the witness's evidence in the Tolimir case, now in evidence in this case, P1654. There are five pages from a notebook that was used by the witness's unit. He discusses the -- that notebook in his -- his written evidence, and he explains that notebook.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is there a whole notebook or only these five pages in existence right now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, is it -- let me just have a look. It is five pages of that notebook as far as I understand, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the pages are not in order. We have 53, 56, 57, 58, and then 71. So we don't know why there are some missing pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's not clear to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, again I think it's explained in the witness's written evidence that pages which correspond to particular intercepts or pages that have entries that correspond to particular intercepts have been extracted from the witness's notebook and for that reason these pages, these five pages, have been tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, is there any wish to add any of the pages in between of those selected by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We don't know. We haven't seen them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has that not been disclosed any earlier? Do you say that it has not been disclosed, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe Miss Janet can help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have five pages from this notebook. Those five pages have been disclosed to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the other pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: We don't have the other pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't have the other pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied, and the 65 ter 05302 is admitted under the provisionally assigned number Exhibit P1670. Next 65 ter 25531. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We object to [microphone not activated] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry. I said we object to this one as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For what reasons?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Drazen Erdemovic was born in Tuzla in 1971 and is of Bosnian Croat descent. He did his mandatory military service with the JNA, which ended in March 1992. He then served for a short time in the Bosnian Muslim Army. He then joined the Bosnian Croat army and left that in November 1993. In April 1994, Mr. Erdemovic joined the VRS and later became a member of the 10th Sabotage Detachment which consisted of two platoons, one in Bijeljina and one in Vlasenica. Mr. Erdemovic was a member of the Bijeljina Platoon. The 10th Sabotage Detachment did reconnaissance and sabotage work behind enemy lines. The unit was directly subordinated to the Main Staff of the VRS. Colonel Petar Salapura, and intelligence officer from the Main Staff, was in charge of the unit, and the unit itself was commanded by 2nd lieutenant Milorad Pelemis. On the afternoon of 10 July, Mr. Erdemovic, together with other members of his unit, travelled from Bratunac towards Srebrenica to take part in the attack on the enclave. They spent the night at an elevation above Srebrenica. On the morning of 11 July, Erdemovic and the members of his unit descended into Srebrenica town. Their commander, Pelemis, told the members of the unit not to harm any civilians but to direct them to the soccer stadium in town. When Mr. Erdemovic and the others reached the centre of Srebrenica town, an able bodied Muslim man surrendered to them. Pelemis ordered a man named Zoran from his unit to kill this man. Erdemovic saw Zoran carry out this order by slitting the man's throat. On the morning of 16 July, Erdemovic and seven other members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment commanded by one of their own, Brano Gojkovic, departed from their base in Dragasevac for Zvornik. At the Zvornik Brigade barracks, a lieutenant-colonel in a VRS uniform came out of the barracks accompanied by two members of the Drina Corps military police, the lieutenant-colonel and the two MPs got in a vehicle and led Erdemovic's group from Zvornik to a farm near the town of Pilica. The lieutenant-colonel was tall, corpulent, with grey hair. The lieutenant-colonel spoke to Brano Gojkovic and told him that buses would be coming to the farm. A short time later, Gojkovic announced that buses carrying civilians from Srebrenica would start arriving and that they were to be killed. At approximately 9.30 to 10.00 a.m. the first bus arrived. A group of approximately 10 prisoners were taken off the bus, blindfolded with their hands tied behind their back. They were taken to a nearby meadow and shot on orders from Brano Gojkovic. Mr. Erdemovic along with the other seven members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment opened fire on the prisoners with automatic weapons. The executions continued in this way from approximately 1000 hours until about 1530 to 1600 hours with 15 to 20 busloads of prisoners ultimately being executed. Mr. Erdemovic estimated that between 1.000 and 1.200 people were executed at the farm that day. Early in the afternoon that day, soldiers in VRS uniform arrived at the farm. Mr. Erdemovic believed these men were from Bratunac and he believed they knew some of the victims by the way they were acting towards them. As the executions progressed, these soldiers beat and cursed the prisoners. Finally, the lieutenant-colonel came back to the farm as the last busload of Muslims were being executed. The lieutenant-colonel told the members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment unit that there were some 500 prisoners at the Pilica cultural centre who also needed to be executed. Mr. Erdemovic, as well as some other members of his squad, refused this order. Instead, members of the unit from Bratunac left the farm with the lieutenant-colonel. Mr. Erdemovic and the others followed to Pilica shortly thereafter. When Mr. Erdemovic and others arrived at Pilica he was across the street from the cultural centre and heard gunfire and hand grenade explosions coming from the cultural centre. And that is the end of the summary.
